lesson_title: The Drawing Pin That Broke the Rules of Chance
hook_text: A coin is 50/50. A spinner is 1-in-8. So what are the odds for a drawing pin? Trick question — you can't count your way there.
clip_script: A drawing pin is nothing like a spinner. Toss it: point-up or point-down, but its shape is all on one side, so no clever counting can predict the split. When theory cannot count, experience has to count instead. So toss it, and toss it, and toss it, keeping a tally. After 250 tosses: 90 point-ups. Experience reports: point-up runs at 90 out of 250 — 0,36. That number, occurrences divided by attempts, is the relative frequency — probability measured rather than reasoned. Toss the pin just 5 times and see 3 point-ups: is point-up really 0,6? Five tosses is a rumour, not evidence. Two hundred and fifty tosses is a report. Two and a half thousand is an audit.
visual_style: Macro shot of a drawing pin tumbling in slow motion, tally marks stacking up on screen, a live fraction ticking from wild swings down to a steady 0,36 as the counter races past 250.
pacing: Quick toss montage, freeze on the tally at 250, slow zoom on the settling number, sharp rumour-report-audit finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to master both probability engines.
